auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.explanation: Row-level security (RLS, Postgres rules that filter which rows each user can see) on the bookings table calls auth.uid(), which identifies the signed-in user, once for every row instead of once per query. This makes booking lookups slower as the table grows, which matters for members checking their own court bookings in the app.
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.impact: Players viewing their own bookings and query speed on health.bookings are affected; access rules are not changed by this fix.
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.fix_summary: Recreate the bookings_own SELECT policy so auth.uid() is wrapped in a scalar subquery, (select auth.uid()), letting Postgres evaluate it once per query while keeping the own-bookings rule unchanged.
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.draft_sql: BEGIN; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS bookings_own ON health.bookings; CREATE POLICY bookings_own ON health.bookings FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (member_id IN (SELECT m.id FROM health.members m WHERE m.user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()))); COMMIT;
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.rollback_sql: BEGIN; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS bookings_own ON health.bookings; CREATE POLICY bookings_own ON health.bookings FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (member_id IN (SELECT m.id FROM health.members m WHERE m.user_id = auth.uid())); COMMIT;

finding.detail: Policy bookings_own on bookings calls auth functions once per row instead of once per query.

duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.explanation: The members table has two indexes on the same column (user_id), so every write to members updates both and the database stores the same lookup data twice. Removing one saves space and write time without changing which queries can run fast, since the remaining index serves the same lookups, including the self-access policy that filters rows by user_id.
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.impact: Club staff and players see no functional change; the benefit is slightly faster inserts and updates on health.members and less index storage.
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.fix_summary: Drop the redundant duplicate index members_user_idx and keep members_user_id_idx, which has the matching naming convention.
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.draft_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.members_user_idx;
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.rollback_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS members_user_idx ON health.members USING btree (user_id);

function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.explanation: This staff-check function runs with the privileges of its owner (SECURITY DEFINER) but does not pin its search_path, which is the list of schemas Postgres searches when resolving names. That means a user who can create objects in an earlier schema on the search path could shadow names the function uses, such as the members table or auth.uid(), and change its result. Pinning the search_path to empty closes that gap, and the function body already uses fully qualified names, so it keeps working.
function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.impact: Club staff permission checks rely on this function, so an attacker who could shadow its lookups could gain or spoof staff access to club member data, and the lint flags the risk as a security warning.
function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.fix_summary: Set the function's search_path to an empty string so every name it uses must be schema-qualified, which it already is.

finding.detail: Function is_staff(p_club uuid) has no fixed search_path and runs as SECURITY DEFINER.

context.function_definition:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION health.is_staff(p_club uuid)
 RETURNS boolean
 LANGUAGE sql
 STABLE SECURITY DEFINER
AS $function$
  select exists (select 1 from health.members m where m.club_id = p_club and m.user_id = auth.uid() and m.role = 'staff')
$function$

permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.explanation: The payments table has a row-level security policy named payments_all that uses a condition of true, so any signed-in user can read every payment row in the database. Courtline's rule is that a player sees only their own payments, and club staff see payments for their club, so this exposes other members' payment records. The fix replaces the open policy with one that enforces that rule.
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.impact: Every signed-in player and any staff account can read all members' payment records across all clubs, which is a privacy and security exposure and an access-control failure for club staff and members.
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.fix_summary: Add a SELECT policy on health.payments that allows a row when the member_id belongs to the signed-in user or the signed-in user is staff for the row's club, then drop the permissive payments_all policy.
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.draft_sql: CREATE POLICY payments_own_or_staff ON health.payments FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (member_id IN (SELECT m.id FROM health.members m WHERE m.user_id = (SELECT auth.uid())) OR health.is_staff(club_id)); DROP POLICY payments_all ON health.payments;
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.rollback_sql: CREATE POLICY payments_all ON health.payments FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (true); DROP POLICY payments_own_or_staff ON health.payments;

finding.detail: Policy payments_all on payments uses USING (true), so every signed-in user sees every row, but Courtline's rule for payments is 'own_or_staff'.

rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.explanation: The leagues table is readable through the public API but has row level security (RLS, Postgres rules that filter which rows each user can see) turned off, so any signed-in user can read every league at every club. Courtline's rule is that league visibility is limited to the club, so members of one club should not see another club's leagues. The fix adds a read policy that only returns rows where the signed-in user is a member of that club.
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.impact: Players at one club can see leagues run by other clubs, which exposes club data to people who should not have access; query speed is not affected.
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.fix_summary: Add a SELECT policy on health.leagues that uses health.is_member(club_id), then enable row level security on the table.
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.draft_sql: CREATE POLICY leagues_select_club_members ON health.leagues FOR SELECT USING (health.is_member(club_id)); ALTER TABLE health.leagues ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.rollback_sql: ALTER TABLE health.leagues DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS leagues_select_club_members ON health.leagues;

unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.explanation: The bookings table has a foreign key called bookings_club_id_fkey linking each booking to its club, but no index covers the club_id column. Without an index, Postgres must scan the whole bookings table whenever a club is deleted or its key is checked, and lookups filtering bookings by club get slower as the table grows.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.impact: Club staff and query speed are affected: club-level operations and deletes on the clubs table can slow down as bookings grow, while player access and security are not changed by this finding.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.fix_summary: Create a b-tree index on health.bookings(club_id) so the foreign key is covered, built without locking writes to the table.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_club_id_idx ON health.bookings (club_id);
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_club_id_idx;

unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.explanation: The bookings table has a foreign key bookings_court_id_fkey linking court_id to a court, but no index starts with court_id. Postgres does not create indexes on foreign key columns automatically, so lookups by court and checks when a court is deleted or changed must scan the whole bookings table. An index on court_id lets Postgres find a court's bookings directly.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.impact: Club staff and players may see slower court availability and booking lookups as bookings grow, and deleting or updating a court can cause slow scans that lock related rows longer.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.fix_summary: Add a non-blocking btree index on health.bookings(court_id) so the foreign key is covered.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_court_id_idx ON health.bookings USING btree (court_id);
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_court_id_idx;

unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.explanation: The bookings table has a foreign key member_id that links each booking to the member who made it, but there is no index on that column. Without an index, Postgres must scan the whole bookings table to find a member's bookings, which slows down lookups such as a member's booking history and also makes deleting or changing a member slower because the database checks for dependent bookings. The row-level security rule for members filters bookings by member_id, so this missing index also affects how quickly each member's own bookings load.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.impact: Members loading their booking history and club staff working with member records may see slower queries as the bookings table grows; no data is exposed or at risk.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.fix_summary: Add a b-tree index on health.bookings(member_id), built concurrently so writes are not blocked during creation.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_member_id_idx ON health.bookings USING btree (member_id);
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_member_id_idx;

slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.explanation: Courtline's bookings table has no index that covers the club and time-range filter, so each lookup of a club's bookings for a date window scans all 200,000 rows. The query runs 120 times and averages 6.776 ms, which adds up to 813.1 ms total. A composite index on (club_id, start_time) lets Postgres jump straight to the right rows in the right order.
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.impact: Club staff and players loading booking schedules see slower responses, and database load grows as the bookings table grows.
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.fix_summary: Add a composite B-tree index on health.bookings (club_id, start_time) built concurrently so the table stays available during creation.
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_club_id_start_time_idx ON health.bookings (club_id, start_time);
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_club_id_start_time_idx;

finding.detail: A query run 120 times averages 6.776 ms because it reads all 200,000 rows of bookings (sequential scan) to filter on club_id, start_time.
